en: The black earth trembled
And smoldered through its depths.
In his rage, the mad brute
Would wrench his battle-gear’s mouth aside.
The creature was no son of man;
He would crush the enemy to dust.
Külchoro attacked the mountain-sized dog,
For he was a lion beyond compare.
The one he would fight was Sarybai;
Such was the foe he faced.
Sparing not his renowned life,
Your wretched, valiant kinsman
Faced the infidel huge as a mountain,
The hero in the fullness of his strength,
Who gnawed apart all he encountered
And swallowed every living soul.
No one who came to face him
Had escaped with life.
He came to wreak ruin in combat
And wrest his people
From the hands of a blessed nation.
The lion Choro gathered his courage:
“I shall slaughter you all.
If I do not slay every last champion,
Leave your people destitute,
And wage the fiercest battle;
If I do not break the backs
Of your men who call themselves heroes;
If I do not massacre your people,
Slaughtering every last soul,
Kill your khans,
And leave your women in black mourning;
If I do not spread slaughter to your borders,
Seize your maidens and women as plunder,
And take every single one;
I bristle in my anger,
And swell as vast as a mountain.
My strength seethes and surges;
Today I roar transformed.
I shall crush every one of your villages,
And load all your gold and silver
For transport toward Jelpiniş.
I am enraged and stand rigid;
If I do not spill your blood like water,
Drink your blood like water,
And quench my thirst;
May I strike down your lower demons
And seize all four kinds of livestock.
If I do not cast a chilling lasso
Over Buurul, whom you would never surrender if asked;
If I do not take as plunder
Your maidens who boast of their beauty,
May I die and cease to be Sarybai,
May I sink into darkness as though never born!
This accursed breed
Does not know it is about to die;
We cannot leave it alive;
That swine can never be redeemed.”
When the infidel, son of a monster,
Saw the hero Choro,
His shout split heads,
And his bellow split stones.
With that thick-muscled dog,
He came forth to confront him.
The one-armed gray-maned lion—
The spirit of Manas appeared openly,
Struck alongside him as a companion,
And openly lent him aid.
They rushed to face each other,
Preparing to meet in combat,
To turn each other’s horses’ heads,
Roaring threateningly,
To charge each other head-on
And test a hero’s courage.
If the true God so willed,
Külchoro would surrender his fly-like soul.
Fierce Külchoro
Unleashed his full courage.
Thinking his poor soul already dead,
He bound it to a hair and cast it away.
The one he faced was Sarybai;
He raised the Syr spear
And rode straight toward him.
Sarybai was a mad brute,
Standing unmoved by its humming flight
And reckoning it no higher than his heel.
Sarybai stood and said:
“Come not as one, but as a thousand;
Come six at once to grapple with me.
When I charge in fury,
My witless Külchoro,
Your eyes will be gouged out!
With Khan Semetey at their head,
Your Seytek too will be slaughtered.
If I do not gouge out your warriors’ eyes
And butcher every one of you;
If I do not fell your plane trees,
Topple and demolish your houses,
And lay waste your encampment;
If I do not herd your khans away captive,
Leaving not a hair’s worth of life;
If I do not destroy every last one of you,
Then I am not hero Sarybai.
Dust rises beneath my tread,
And souls depart at my thunder.
I am the black eye of the Antichrist,
The monster himself.
Give me the slightest chance and I shall slaughter you;
Neither Semetey nor Choro—
Today I shall not be sated
By all eighteen thousand worlds.
When I charge in fury,
I become an irresistible flood.
Khans die beneath your sweeping blow;
Everyone you meet dies.
I am mighty, I am the strongest,
So formidable am I.
I am the black eye of the Antichrist,
Sarybai himself.
To anyone who takes my measure,
I am a fortress walled in steel.
Known as Sarybai’s son,
I am famed among many peoples.
I am calamity itself,
The black eye of the Antichrist.
I am doom to those who walk at ease,
A true taker of souls.
I strike down the majestic;
When angered, I devour the world
Like a dragon.
My terrible fury has seized me;
I shall slaughter you
Without leaving a single hair.”
Uttering many dreadful words,
He stood there shouting.
Now perfect God struck
The infidel, son of a monster.
The mad brute made the earth sag;
Under the infidel’s might
The ground seemed to split apart.
When he beheld the monster’s son,
Armed with his great musket,
Such was his appearance when measured.
He could not keep from raging;
Sarybai ground his formidable teeth
Again and again.
His lashes blazed and turned to embers;
Among men there was none
Like the ill-fated infidel.
“I shall defeat your nobles
And swallow your whole clan.
I shall utterly slaughter your people;
If I do not break your back,
Strip away your strength,
And make your blood flow like water,
Leaving not even your written trace,
I shall grind you all to dust.
You accursed wretch, you will never prosper;
Never, from one age to the next,
Will you abandon your defiance.
Abandon all hope for your life;
What use is your rage?
Not one hair of you will remain;
You will be massacred.
I shall inflict hell upon you all
And engulf your village in ruin.
Yesterday I stiffened in fury
And slaughtered many giants.
Without sparing a single one,
I put them all to the sword.
Of those who dared oppose me,
On the blood of many giants
I, Khan Sarybai, have feasted.
Whole peoples died by provoking my wrath,
And many formidable champions died.
I mow down all who cross my path;
I am a bolt of black steel,
Without equal in the world.
I gnaw apart all whom I meet;
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
I am a towering hero.
I have made the whole world my slave,
He had grown hardened from drinking blood,
Seasoned by constant combat.
Having pledged himself to the twelve holy patrons,
He was named Külchoro the Lion.
Among spearmen, Külchoro
Was a surpassingly renowned and able man,
Who knew better than any
How to outwit the enemy he fought.
A man wise in all the world,
A hunter who seized like a falcon.
Breaking through dead ends and opening roads,
Against the infidel son of a monster,
Against the hero Er Sarybai,
If fate decreed that he should die,
If God truly willed it,
He would surrender his fly-like soul.
He would go and thrust his spear,
And sacrifice his reckless life,
Trading blows if he had the strength,
And stand face-to-face with him.
Then Choro resolved upon this:
Against the grim-faced infidel
He would charge straight in and level his spear,
For God, for the people,
For the rugged Ala-Too,
For the Kyrgyz people of the north,
Who dwelt in the Ala-Too.
Choro, noblest of kinsmen,
Choro the hero, upheld by the saints,
Terrible in bearing, mighty in wrath,
Choro the hero who spared no one,
Choro, favored by perfect fortune,
Who straightened all who challenged him—
Such was Külchoro’s nature.
Taking his steel spear in hand,
He attacked Sarybai,
Power radiating from his presence,
While between his two cheeks
Grew whiskers five finger-widths long.
Sarybai confronted him,
And Külchoro, a blazing ember,
Prayed to the Creator:
“Grant us abundance while we live,
And grant us faith if we die.
We are not mere brushwood—do not make us a road.
We are sons of princes—
Do not disgrace us before the dog Sarybai!”
Ask no more about Külchoro:
He was a glowing crimson ember,
A bullet of steel against the foe.
When he charged in fury,
There was none like him in all the world.
Choro, proud of his valor,
Against the infidel son of a monster,
Buckled his battle sash around his waist,
And against that earth-smeared swine
He went alone and attacked.
He pulled the reins
And turned the mouth of his fluid-swift Surat.
Against the roaring infidel
He leveled his spear with a roar.
Such was Külchoro’s way;
Sarybai charged,
And this was how he prepared:
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both wrestler and lion,
Both mighty and heroic,
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A reckless man of boundless courage,
Who throughout the eighteen thousand worlds
Had stirred up great turmoil.
His lashes were flame, his eyes embers.
No other man possessed such dreadfulness.
He brought turmoil upon his foes;
